cls: Iron-based phosphate binder (non-calcium, non-aluminum) for hyperphosphatemia in CKD on dialysis
pharm: Chewable iron-based phosphate binder. In the GI tract, polynuclear iron(III)-oxyhydroxide binds dietary phosphate by ligand exchange, and the bound phosphate is eliminated in the feces, lowering serum phosphorus. It is essentially non-absorbed and works locally in the gut.
quick: One 500 mg (iron) chewable tablet three times daily WITH meals; titrate by one tablet/day (usual 1,500-2,000 mg/day)
Take WITH meals and chew or crush (do not swallow whole) - it binds dietary phosphate
Not systemically absorbed; maternal use not expected to cause fetal exposure
Not absorbed systemically; not expected to expose the breastfed infant
Indicated specifically for CKD patients on dialysis; no extra renal dose adjustment
Not studied in significant hepatic disorders; monitor effect and iron homeostasis
No specific interaction described in labeling
Serum phosphorus (titrate as often as weekly), and iron homeostasis in at-risk patients
summary: Sucroferric oxyhydroxide (Velphoro) is an iron-based, calcium-free, aluminum-free PHOSPHATE BINDER used to control serum phosphorus levels in adults and children 9 years and older with chronic kidney disease (CKD) on dialysis. It works locally in the gastrointestinal tract: polynuclear iron(III)-oxyhydroxide binds dietary phosphate by ligand exchange so the phosphate is excreted in the feces rather than absorbed. It is supplied as 500 mg iron (equivalent to 2,500 mg sucroferric oxyhydroxide) chewable tablets. The usual starting dose in adults and patients >=12 years is one 500 mg tablet three times daily WITH meals, with the tablet chewed or crushed (never swallowed whole). The most common adverse reactions are discolored (black) feces and diarrhea. There are no formal contraindications in labeling. Iron from the product is minimally absorbed, so systemic iron toxicity risk is low.

moa: In the aqueous environment of the GI tract, phosphate binding takes place by ligand exchange between hydroxyl groups and/or water in sucroferric oxyhydroxide and the phosphate in the diet. The bound phosphate is then eliminated in the feces. As a result, dietary phosphate absorption is reduced, lowering both serum phosphorus and the calcium-phosphorus product. The active moiety, polynuclear iron(III)-oxyhydroxide, is practically insoluble in water and is essentially not absorbed and not metabolized, so the drug acts locally within the gut.

preg: Velphoro is not systemically absorbed following oral administration, and maternal use is not expected to result in fetal exposure to the drug. In animal reproduction studies, no embryo-fetal developmental toxicity was seen in rats at up to 16 times the maximum recommended clinical dose; in rabbits, incomplete/unossified bones were increased only at the highest dose (about 4 times the maximum clinical dose) without effect on litter parameters.
lact: Velphoro is not absorbed systemically following oral administration, and breastfeeding is not expected to result in exposure of the breastfed child to the drug.
renal: Velphoro is indicated specifically for the control of serum phosphorus in CKD patients on dialysis; no additional dose adjustment for renal impairment is specified beyond titrating to serum phosphorus. Notably, iron uptake from the product is even lower in CKD patients than in healthy subjects.
hepatic: Patients with significant hepatic disorders were not included in clinical studies. Monitor effect and iron homeostasis in such patients; no specific dosage adjustment is provided.

major: Levothyroxine - take at least 4 hours before Velphoro (reduced thyroid hormone absorption)
moderate: Doxycycline, acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin), cephalexin - take at least 1 hour before Velphoro
Other oral drugs with a narrow therapeutic range or where reduced bioavailability would be clinically significant - consider separating administration and monitoring response/levels
minor: No interaction shown with calcitriol, ciprofloxacin, digoxin, enalapril, furosemide, HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors, hydrochlorothiazide, losartan, metoprolol, nifedipine, omeprazole, quinidine, or warfarin (may be co-administered)
interactions.food: Must be taken WITH meals to bind dietary phosphate; this is essential to its mechanism, not an adverse interaction.
interactions.alcohol: No specific interaction with alcohol described in the labeling.
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor serum phosphorus to guide titration; monitor iron homeostasis (e.g., iron indices) in patients with iron accumulation disorders.

common: Diarrhea (often mild, transient, occurring soon after initiation and resolving with continued treatment)
serious: Persistent or severe diarrhea leading to treatment withdrawal (uncommon)
rare: Potential iron accumulation in patients with predisposing iron-storage disorders (theoretical; iron absorption is low)
emergency: Severe dehydration from significant diarrhea, particularly relevant in dialysis patients

pearls: Iron-based, calcium-free and aluminum-free PHOSPHATE BINDER for control of serum phosphorus in CKD patients on dialysis - works in the gut, not systemically
Each chewable tablet = 500 mg iron, equivalent to 2,500 mg sucroferric oxyhydroxide; chew or crush and take WITH meals
Discolored (black) feces (~12-16%) and diarrhea (~6-24%) are the most common adverse reactions; black stool is expected and benign
Low pill burden is an advantage - average effective dose is only 3-4 tablets/day to control phosphorus
No formal contraindications; iron absorption is very low (even lower in CKD patients), so systemic iron toxicity risk is low
Separate levothyroxine by >=4 hours and aspirin/cephalexin/doxycycline by >=1 hour
missed: If one or more doses are missed, resume the medication with the next food intake (next meal). Do not take a dose without food, since the tablet must be taken with a meal to bind dietary phosphate. Do not double up.
overdose: There are no reports of overdosage in patients. Because iron absorption from Velphoro is low, the risk of systemic iron toxicity is low. Hypophosphatemia from excessive phosphate binding should be treated by standard clinical practice. Doses up to 3,000 mg per day have been studied.
